Issued at 122 AM CDT Tue Sep 8 2026

As an upper-level trough continues to push east today, it will be 
suppressing the upper-level ridge that has be stuck over SD. This 
upper-level trough will continue to help a cold front at the surface 
finish moving through northeastern SD during the morning. There is a 
little bit of warm air and moisture trying to advect into portions 
of south central and northeastern SD in front of the the cold front 
early this morning. The warm air and moisture advecting in as well 
as a weak low level jet sitting over the area again is creating some 
more of the elevated scattered showers and storms, similar to what 
has been happening the past few mornings. These showers and storms 
will have a little bit of shear and some lapse rates, around 5-6 
C/km, to strengthen a bit, though they should stay below severe 
criteria. As the cold front moves through this morning, these 
showers and storms should dissipate as dry air moves in. 

Behind the cold front, some high surface pressure will move through 
southwestern SD while a low pressure sits over Manitoba and 
Saskatchewan, which will help to create a tight pressure gradient 
over ND and northern SD. This tight pressure gradient will cause 
stronger winds to develop aloft, and with stronger lapse rates and 
cold air advection occurring, there will be a fair bit of mixing in 
the atmosphere to get these winds down to the surface over 
north central SD. The ensembles have a 30-50% chance for the 
northwest winds to gust around and greater than 40 mph, and 50-80% 
chance for 35+ mph wind gusts over mainly Corson and Dewey counties. 
The HREF models has slightly weaker winds chances over north central 
SD, with a 40-80% chance for winds to gust greater than 30 mph. 
While these winds are weaker than wind advisory criteria, they are a 
big point of concern for fire weather in portions of north central 
SD. There is a 20-40% chance that conditions mainly in Dewey county 
but also other portions of north central SD will reach Red Flag 
criteria, which is wind gusts greater than 25 mph and relative 
humidity values less than 20% in addition to dry fuels. The main 
cause for these lower chances is because the humidity values will be 
slightly above 20%. When checking the models for wind gusts greater 
than 25 mph and humidity less than 25%, then the chances shoot up to 
50-80% over Dewey county and slightly lower over other portions of 
north central SD. While the conditions do not reach Red Flag 
criteria, there is still Very High to High Grassland Fire Danger 
Index Values and some fire weather concerns for Dewey, Corson, and 
other portions of north central SD this afternoon. With the dry 
fuels in these areas in combination with the weather conditions, if 
a fire were to ignite, it would become difficult to suppress or 
control. 

Temperatures today behind the cold front will be around to just 
slightly above normal for this time of the year, in the upper 70s to 
mid 80s. Another surface cold front is forecast to move through SD 
again tonight into early Wednesday morning. The RAP model shows 
there to be a little bit of instability over portions of northern SD 
tonight, with CAPE values less than 1000 J/kg, as well as a little 
bit of lingering moisture aloft. The cold front could interact with 
this environment during the overnight hours into Wednesday morning 
to create some isolated to scattered showers and storms over 
portions of central and northeastern SD. While there will be a fair 
bit of shear from the frontal boundaries, the lapse rates will be a 
bit weaker. This will help the showers and storms from becoming 
severe. However, with the stronger shear, around 45-60 kts, even 
some weaker lapse rates could get strong winds to the surface and 
the storms could have gusts up around 50 mph. 

The second cold front will help to cool temperatures even more on 
Wednesday, with highs in the 70s possible. A weak upper-level ridge 
will be moving over SD Thursday and Friday, which will help to move 
some warm, drier air in again, with highs these day in the low 80s 
to low 90s. A surface high pressure moving in Wednesday afternoon 
through Thursday night along with the drier air aloft will help to 
keep showers and storms from developing for a couple of days. The 
next chances for precipitation will be during the day and evening 
Friday as another frontal boundary moves through.
